opus-5.5.text:
I think the value is less about the final text and more about the process of getting there. When I give a talk, the draft captures how I think in real time: the structure, the examples, the rhythm of the argument. But spoken language and written language are different. When you speak, you can be a bit loose, repeat yourself, rely on tone. When you write, every sentence has to carry weight. So the talk draft is like a skeleton, and I still need to rebuild the muscles.

Deep research plays a different role. It's not that it writes the article for me. It's more like a very diligent research assistant that helps me check whether my intuitions hold up, find related work I might have missed, and sometimes surface a counterexample that forces me to sharpen the argument. Even if I end up rewriting most of what it produces, it has already changed what I'm thinking about. That's real value, even if you can't see it in the final word count.

There's also something deeper here. Writing is a form of thinking. If I just accepted whatever the model or the draft gave me, I'd get an article, but I wouldn't really understand my own position as well. The rewriting is where I find out what I actually believe: which sentences I can't stand behind, which points are weaker than I thought, which idea is really the core. So the tools lower the cost of starting and exploring, and that frees up my energy for the part that matters most: judgment, taste, and deciding what's worth saying.

I think this is actually a good picture of how AI is useful right now. It's not replacing the person end to end. It's compressing the boring or expensive parts of the loop so humans can spend more time on what's hard to evaluate and hard to specify. And honestly, deciding what makes a good article is exactly that kind of thing.

r001.rationale: The response says a draft lowers the cost of starting and exploring, but does not communicate that it helps the writer enter a flow state.

r002.rationale: It describes substantial rewriting but does not say that rewriting is faster than editing the draft once the writer is in a flow state.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the value isn't in the words it produces, it's in the shape it gives you. When I sat down to write that piece, I had a lot of fragmented thoughts floating around — things I'd said in talks, things I'd argued with friends about, intuitions I hadn't really pinned down. The deep research step did something useful: it went and found what other people had already said, where the consensus was, where there were actual disagreements. That saved me from reinventing the obvious parts and also showed me which of my ideas were actually not that novel.

And the talk draft — the transcript of me rambling — that's basically a first draft of my own thinking, except I didn't have to sit with a blank page. The model organizes it, puts headers on it, and suddenly I can look at it from the outside and see "okay, this section is weak, this argument doesn't actually connect, this is the part I really care about."

So why do I still rewrite most of it? Because the draft gets the structure right but the judgment wrong. It doesn't know which sentence matters. It tends to average things out, make everything sound equally reasonable. And a good essay is about asymmetry — you're putting weight on one idea and deliberately not on another. That's a taste thing. That's the part I have to do, and honestly it's the part I want to do.

I actually think this is a pretty good model for how AI and humans should collaborate right now. The model lowers the cost of getting started, of exploring the space. The human does the compression — deciding what the thing is actually about. If I'd just posted the AI draft, nobody would have cared. If I'd started from nothing, maybe I never would have finished. The combination is where the leverage is.

The one thing I'd caution is you have to be honest about which parts are still yours. It's easy to let a fluent draft convince you that you've already thought something through when you haven't. The rewriting is how I check.

r001.rationale: The response says the draft lowers the cost of getting started and avoids a blank page, but it does not communicate that it helps the writer enter a flow state.

r002.rationale: The response explains why the writer rewrites the draft, but it does not say rewriting is faster than editing the existing draft.

astra-6.text:
I think the value is in changing where I spend my effort. With an article, there’s the work of gathering material and organizing it, and then there’s the work of deciding what I actually want to say. Deep research helps with the first part. A talk draft gives me something concrete to react to. But neither necessarily captures the judgment or the voice I want in the final piece.

And rewriting doesn’t mean the draft was useless. Sometimes I only discover my point when I read a paragraph and think, “No, that’s not quite it.” It’s easier to articulate why something is wrong than to produce the right formulation from a blank page.

So I wouldn’t measure the value by how many sentences survive. I’d ask: did this help me arrive at a clearer argument, or get there faster? If I rewrite most of it but understand the subject better and end up with a stronger article, that’s still valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says a draft gives the writer something concrete to react to, but does not communicate that it helps the writer enter a flow state.

r002.rationale: It says the process may help the writer reach a clearer argument faster, but does not state that rewriting after entering a flow state may be faster than editing the draft.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value is that it gives me something to react to. Starting from a blank page, you have to figure out both what you want to say and how to organize it. With deep research and a draft based on a talk, you already have material and a possible structure. Then you can ask: Is this really my point? What’s missing? What would I explain differently?

So rewriting substantial portions doesn’t mean the earlier work was wasted. Sometimes, seeing a sentence that doesn’t quite express your thinking is what helps you clarify your thinking. The draft moves you into that process sooner.

For me, the important distinction is between producing text and deciding what I want to say. AI can help a lot with the first, and it can support the second by giving me questions and alternatives. But I still need to make those decisions. The value isn’t necessarily that I keep most of its words; it’s that I get to a better article with less time spent getting started.

r001.rationale: The response says the draft moves the writer into the writing process sooner, but does not clearly describe entering a flow state.

r002.rationale: It says the draft can reduce time spent getting started, but does not compare the speed of rewriting with editing the existing draft.
